title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Trisomy 13, also known as Patau syndrome, is a chromosomal aneuploidy most often caused by meiotic nondisjunction and characterized by an extra copy of chromosome 13. The condition disrupts early embryologic development, particularly involving the prechordal mesoderm, resulting in abnormal midline patterning. Common phenotypic features include holoprosencephaly, craniofacial anomalies, congenital heart disease, central nervous system malformations, and severe multisystem involvement. Trisomy 13 is associated with high rates of neonatal morbidity and mortality, with survival beyond infancy being uncommon. Diagnosis may occur prenatally through ultrasonography, noninvasive prenatal testing, and confirmatory cytogenetic analysis, or postnatally based on clinical findings and karyotype evaluation. Management focuses on supportive, palliative, and family-centered care, guided by prognosis and individual goals of care.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance clinicians' competence in recognizing, diagnosing, and managing trisomy 13 across prenatal and postnatal settings. Participants gain a deeper understanding of genetic mechanisms, epidemiology, clinical presentation, and diagnostic strategies, including appropriate use and interpretation of screening and confirmatory tests. The curriculum emphasizes prognosis, differential diagnosis, and ethical considerations, including goals-of-care discussions and recurrence risk counseling. Collaboration among an interprofessional healthcare team, including genetics, neonatology, cardiology, palliative care, and counseling services, is highlighted as essential for coordinated decision-making, effective family communication, and improved patient-centered outcomes.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Introduction
content: Trisomy 13 is a chromosomal aneuploidy originally described by Patau et al in 1960. The incidence of trisomy 13 is 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 live births, with antenatal mortality exceeding 95% of gestations. [1] [2] This condition can occur as a complete, partial, or mosaic expression. Complete trisomy is the most common presentation, accounting for about 80% of patients. This expression characteristically shows 3 copies of chromosome 13. Partial trisomy 13 most commonly results from a Robertsonian translocation, typically involving chromosomes 13 and 14 [t(13;14)]. Mosaic trisomy 13, accounting for approximately 5% of cases, arises postzygotically and is characterized by a mixture of euploid and trisomic cells. [3] [4]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Introduction
content: Trisomy 13 arises from nondisjunction of germ cells during meiosis I or II in either parental cell line. [5] Nonetheless, maternal meiotic nondisjunction, associated with increased maternal age at conception, accounts for approximately 91% of trisomy 13 cases. [2] Complete trisomy 13 most commonly results from sporadic meiotic nondisjunction, typically arising during maternal gametogenesis. In contrast, familial inheritance of trisomy 13 occurs in a minority of cases and is usually due to a balanced Robertsonian translocation in 1 parent, which can be vertically transmitted and result in partial or complete trisomy 13 in the offspring. [5]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Introduction
content: Phenotypic findings in trisomy 13 include patterns of congenital anomalies and profound neurodevelopmental impairment, typically incompatible with long-term survival. [5] The embryological defects in trisomy 13 develop in the absence of prechordal mesoderm fusion, which phenotypically manifests as midline defects. These midline defects are associated with aberrant SHH genes. [6] Despite the high mortality associated with trisomy 13, it remains clinically significant because patients with mosaic trisomy 13 can exhibit variable expressivity and survive longer. [3]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Etiology
content: Trisomy 13 results from the nondisjunction of homologous chromosomes during gametogenesis, characterized by 3 copies of chromosome 13 in both somatic and germ cell lines. [5] Maternal nondisjunction represents 91% of cases, typically due to errors in meiosis I. Meiotic errors arise from aberrant chromosome recombination, which is more common in conceptions among women aged 35 or older. [2]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Etiology
content: A less severe phenotypic presentation of trisomy 13 can occur in cases caused by a Robertsonian translocation. These originate from 2 acrocentric breaks in the juxtacentromeric regions (usually chromosomes 13 and 14). Phenotypic expression depends on the balance of the translocation. Balanced Robertsonian translocations are less severe than those with altered genetic quantity, as seen in unbalanced translocations. [7] The mosaic form of trisomy 13 occurs when some cell lines have extra chromosomal material. [5] Mosaicism phenotype presents with variable expressivity and increased intellectual sparing. [3]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Epidemiology
content: Trisomy 13 is the third most common autosomal trisomy, occurring in approximately 1 in 10,000 to 20,000 live births. [1] In high-resource countries, the majority of diagnoses are made prenatally, with about 90% identified before birth. [8] Advanced maternal age is a well-recognized risk factor, consistent with meiotic nondisjunction as the primary etiology. [9] Postnatal survival is limited, with only 6% to 12% of infants surviving beyond the first year of life; more prolonged survival has been reported in cases of mosaic or partial trisomy. [10]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Pathophysiology
content: Meiotic nondisjunction in trisomy 13 causes a series of genetic aberrations related to defects in prechordal mesoderm fusion. [6] The faulty fusion leads to midline defects that progress to phenotypic malformations incompatible with life. Cellular aneuploidy also affects fundamental processes such as proliferation and viability, with evidence suggesting that cells with extra chromosomal material exhibit altered growth and developmental dynamics compared with euploid cells. [11] Specific genetic mapping has identified a wide range of tumors in trisomy 13 carriers. [1]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Histopathology
content: In 1966, Snodgrass and colleagues proposed an anatomic–histologic classification of trisomy 13, dividing cases into 2 categories based on the presence or absence of holoprosencephaly. Further evaluation often reveals postaxial hexadactyly. Midline malformations of internal organs are common and include septal cardiac defects and Müllerian anomalies, such as uterus didelphys. Microscopic examination of aborted fetuses with trisomy 13 demonstrates abnormal metanephric differentiation with persistence of embryonic structures. Many of the associated embryologic abnormalities are attributable to disrupted mesodermal migration, as illustrated by olfactory aplasia; normal craniofacial and forebrain morphogenesis occur during the third week of embryogenesis. [12]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- History and Physical
content: Infants with trisomy 13 are typically born with low birth weight and are frequently small for gestational age. [5] [13] The condition is characterized by multiple midline anomalies, including congenital heart defects (57%-80%), cleft lip and/or palate (45%), holoprosencephaly spectrum anomalies (74%), and postaxial polydactyly (63%-67%). [14] [15] [16] Holoprosencephaly is a failure of the prosencephalon (forebrain) to divide into 2 cerebral hemispheres during early embryonic development. Severity ranges from alobar holoprosencephaly (complete failure of separation) to milder forms such as lobar holoprosencephaly. Associated facial anomalies often accompany these brain malformations, including hypotelorism, microphthalmia or anophthalmia (53%-60%), cyclopia, micrognathia (50%), abnormal auricles (77%), cutis aplasia of the scalp, and midline facial clefts. [16] [17] [18] Neurologic abnormalities are universal, with brain or spinal cord malformations present, and infants with trisomy 13 have severe neurocognitive impairment, usually with hypotonia. [14] [15] Cardiac defects occur in 76% to 90% of cases and include atrial septal defects, ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and hypoplastic left heart. [14] [18]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- History and Physical
content: Additional findings include: Genitourinary: Cryptorchidism (78%), renal anomalies (71%), anogenital abnormalities (60%) [15] [19] Abdominal: Omphalocele [16] Skeletal: Duplication or triplication of the distal phalanx of the thumb or hallux (38% in fetal series) [17] Mosaic trisomy 13 (20% of cases) typically presents with milder features and variable expressivity, though the phenotype does not always correlate with the percentage of trisomic cells. [20]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Evaluation
content: The prenatal evaluation of trisomy 13 begins with an ultrasound examination to assess fetal nuchal translucency, performed between weeks 11 and 14 of gestation. As with other trisomies, this measurement is typically greater than or equal to 3.5 mm. First-trimester screening also includes measuring free beta-subunit or total human chorionic gonadotropin and pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A. In the first trimester, both biomarkers are often decreased and do not reliably distinguish trisomy 13 from trisomy 18. [21]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Evaluation
content: Noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) using cell-free fetal DNA in maternal plasma can distinguish trisomy 13 from trisomies 18 and 21 and is widely regarded as a cost-effective alternative to invasive diagnostic procedures in general-risk populations. The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics recommends NIPT as the preferred first-line screening test for trisomies 13, 18, and 21 in all pregnant patients with singleton gestations. [22] [23] Diagnostic confirmation may also be obtained prenatally through chorionic villus sampling, typically performed between 11 and 13 weeks' gestation, or amniocentesis, typically performed between 15 and 18 weeks' gestation. [5] Both procedures carry a small but measurable risk of pregnancy loss, estimated at approximately 0.1% to 0.3%.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Evaluation
content: A definitive prenatal diagnosis of trisomy 13 can be made by invasive testing, such as karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis. Results from recent studies suggest that the high prenatal and perinatal mortality reported for trisomies 13 and 18 is partly related to elective pregnancy termination after confirmed diagnosis, occurring in up to 55% of affected pregnancies. [24] Postnatal diagnosis of trisomy 13 by karyotyping and fluorescence in situ hybridization is performed when the condition is not identified prenatally. This may result from absent or limited prenatal care; an intentional decision by expectant parents to forgo genetic screening or detailed fetal ultrasonography; a preference to defer diagnostic confirmation until after birth; or obstetric and fetal factors—such as suboptimal imaging conditions or a relatively mild fetal phenotype—that limit prenatal detection. [14]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Treatment / Management
content: The care of infants with trisomy 13 is highly individualized and has evolved beyond an exclusively comfort-focused approach to a broader spectrum of supportive and selectively interventional care. Historically, the presence of multiple severe congenital anomalies in trisomy 13 and trisomy 18 was considered uniformly incompatible with life. More recently, increased societal awareness and reports of longer-term survival have challenged this assumption, introducing ethical and clinical complexity into decision-making. [25] Contemporary data indicate a shift in practice toward carefully selected interventions—such as nutritional support, respiratory assistance, and, in some cases, surgical management—guided by the infant's clinical stability, underlying phenotype, and the family's values and goals for care. This evolving approach reflects recognition that some children, particularly those with mosaic or partial trisomy 13, may experience extended survival and potential quality-of-life benefits when management is individualized and aligned with the family's preferences. [10] [26]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Treatment / Management
content: The current approach emphasizes a collaborative partnership between parents and clinicians, with shared decision-making that includes discussions of the child's anticipated quality of life and individualized treatment options tailored to the specific pattern and severity of congenital anomalies. [27] A team approach is central to contemporary management, involving neonatology, cardiology, pulmonology, nutrition, palliative care, and genetics to address complex care needs and optimize quality of life. Supportive therapies often include aggressive management of respiratory compromise with ventilatory support or tracheostomy when appropriate, feeding support via tube feeding or gastrostomy, and careful monitoring and treatment of seizures and other neurologic complications. In select infants with operable congenital cardiac defects or other severe anatomic malformations, surgical intervention may be considered based on overall prognosis, clinical stability, and family preferences, with careful ethical deliberation. At the same time, early involvement of palliative care facilitates symptom control and psychosocial support for families and aligns care plans with parental values, including advance care planning and the family's goals. [28] [29] [30] Although surgical techniques exist for the majority of lethal malformations associated with trisomy 13, the 10-year survival post-intervention remains low at 12.9%. [31]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of trisomy 13 should include trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome), given its similarities during initial gestational screening. [21] Other diagnoses to rule out include partial duplication of 13q and pseudotrisomy 13. [32] The use of modern noninvasive techniques facilitates prenatal diagnosis of other conditions that share characteristics with trisomy 13. [22]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Prognosis
content: Evidence suggests that postnatal mortality is approximately 50% during the first month and up to 90% during the first year. [3] Recent information from organizations such as the support groups for trisomy 13, 18, and related disorders has enabled direct patient intervention rather than palliative care. [5] These measures have affected patient survival; however, limited data support the benefits of aggressive intervention and global survival rates.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Complications
content: Maternal complications occur more frequently in trisomy 13 pregnancies and contribute to increased morbidity for both the pregnant mother and the fetus. These pregnancies show a higher prevalence of preeclampsia and preterm delivery. [33] Neonatal mortality primarily results from central apnea, severe congenital cardiac malformations, pulmonary hypertension, aspiration, and upper airway obstruction. [5]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Prenatal integration of a multidisciplinary team can improve both maternal outcomes and gestational management in pregnancies affected by trisomy 13. The evaluation team often includes an obstetrician, a perinatal nurse coordinator, a genetic counselor, a neonatologist, the family's pediatrician, and a social worker. [24] Counseling of expectant parents should address the mode of inheritance, potential maternal and fetal complications, anticipated neonatal outcomes, and the benefits and limitations of available postnatal interventions.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Pearls and other issues related to trisomy 13 include the following: Trisomy 13 is the third most common form of nondisjunction meiotic triploidy, after trisomies 21 and 18. [3] The 3 genetic presentations are complete nondisjunction trisomy 13, a Robertsonian translocation, and mosaicism. The most common cause of holoprosencephaly is trisomy 13. [3] During first-trimester screening for trisomy 13, fetal nuchal translucency is equal to or greater than 3.5 mm, with decreased beta human chorionic gonadotropin and pregnancy-associated plasma protein A. [21] Most gestations with trisomy 13 are terminated; the continuation of pregnancy increases the risk of preeclampsia. [33]

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal care for patients with trisomy 13 requires a coordinated interprofessional approach that integrates clinical expertise, ethical decision-making, and effective communication to support patient-centered outcomes and ensure safety. Physicians and advanced practice clinicians lead diagnostic evaluation, prognostication, and shared decision-making, ensuring that care plans align with family goals, clinical realities, and ethical standards. Nurses play a central role in ongoing assessment, symptom management, caregiver education, and patient advocacy, particularly in neonatal intensive care and palliative care settings. [29] Pharmacists contribute by optimizing medication regimens for seizure control, pain management, and other supportive therapies while minimizing adverse effects in medically fragile infants.

title: Trisomy 13 (Patau Syndrome)  -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Genetic counselors, social workers, palliative care specialists, and chaplains address informed consent, psychosocial support, advance care planning, and goals-of-care discussions across the prenatal and postnatal continuum. Consistent interprofessional communication, regular team meetings, and coordinated care transitions enhance continuity of care, reduce errors, and promote compassionate, high-quality care for patients with trisomy 13 and their families. Prenatal counseling has been associated with a decreased reliance on intensive life-prolonging interventions and increased incorporation of palliative care approaches tailored to neonatal comfort and family preferences. [24]
